A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.

The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.

In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.

More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."

"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."

Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."

Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6581. Dakota Johnson Dons Diamonds and a Hoodie for Date Night With Machine Gun Kelly

Dakota Johnson has always had a certain rock-and-roll sensibility to her style, be it the perfectly undone hair, the flash of skin amid the lace and monochromatic, a suite of very good denim. But lately, as her rumored romance with Machine Gun Kelly seems to be gathering momentum, the actor looks to be leaning a little further into her rock-star era. And what better way to do so than with a hoodie and six figures worth of diamonds?

On Thursday evening, Johnson attended a Khaite-hosted dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood, where she was also spotted with Kelly. For the occasion, she mixed the decidedly high and low: a black zip-up hoodie emblazoned with the red logo of Death Row Pictures, Snoop Dogg’s production company, worn over a black Valentino crepe miniskirt with delicate lace trimming. She added a pair of knee-high black Gucci Horsebit boots and a quilted Valentino Rockstud Spike shoulder bag.

Johnson then layered a tiger’s-eye and diamond necklace by Laoli, complete with a diamond clasp pendant, with Jessica McCormack’s Signature 42-carat Diamond Button Back Necklace. (McCormack being the cool-girl jeweler also beloved by Zoe Kravitz.) It brought serious sparkle to an otherwise off-duty ensemble.

Machine Gun Kelly, meanwhile, wore an emerald-green satin bomber jacket over a bright yellow hoodie, with loose gray sweatpants, a black beanie, and a red bandana pulled across his face. The pair, who reportedly left the restaurant separately, might have very different approaches to getting dressed, but there’s an increasingly complementary spirit in their shared taste for casual, slightly rebellious pieces.

Their romance has been unfolding relatively quietly since September, when they were photographed at mutual friend Taylor Swift’s New York apartment. The two reportedly grew closer after attending Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July, and have since made a handful of public appearances in one another’s orbit. At Vogue World: Milano, Kelly walked the runway in a bright orange Byblos jumpsuit while Johnson watched from the front row in plunging black Valentino. More recently, they were photographed leaving a Los Angeles recording studio together, Johnson in her usual uniform of straight-leg jeans, ballet flats, and a long leather coat, before heading off in Kelly’s red sports car. They've also been spotted at the Chateau Marmont and, earlier this week, enjoying another dinner date in Calabasas, where both opted for leather jackets.

Neither has publicly confirmed the nature of their relationship, although their increasingly frequent outings suggest they’re enjoying one another’s company. As for Dakota Johnson’s enviable wardrobe, she’s hardly a stranger to the more provocative side of fashion. Valentino, in particular, has long provided her with a means of balancing romantic femininity with something a little darker and more subversive. And while her love of lace, abbreviated hemlines, and slouchy outerwear predates Kelly, the musician’s punkish influence is there.

#6580. Copycat Coopers Hawk Red Wine–Braised Short Ribs

This copycat Cooper's Hawk red wine-braised short ribs recipe delivers fall-apart-tender short ribs bathed in a luxurious sauce. It's like dining out in your kitchen.

One taste of the red wine–braised short ribs at Cooper’s Hawk is enough to understand why they’ve remained a bestseller. A generous portion of melt-in-your-mouth braised short ribs is stacked over a mound of buttery whipped potatoes, then drizzled with umami-rich braising liquid. When served with roasted vegetables and garnished with crispy fried onion strings, it’s a plate of comfort food that’s just as much a feast for the eyes as it is for the taste buds.

Whether you’ve been to Cooper’s Hawk and want to recreate the magic at home, or you don’t live near a Cooper’s Hawk location and want to know what all the fuss is about, this copycat recipe belongs on your must-try list. It’s the perfect recipe for chilly days when you want a meal that feels like a warm hug. It’s also impressive-looking and great for feeding a crowd, so keep it in mind as the holiday season approaches.

Cooper’s Hawk Winery and Restaurant is something like a more refined Cheesecake Factory that’s known for its wine rather than its cheesecake. Let me break it down. First, each chain greets diners by showcasing its specialties: Where the Cheesecake Factory has cases of cheesecake, Cooper’s Hawk has a well-appointed wine shop. Second, both are known for extensive menus that span a wide range of global influences and cuisines. Finally, both have a long list of signature dishes (we’ve replicated many Cheesecake Factory copycat recipes over the years) that keep customers coming back. These copycat Cooper’s Hawk red wine–braised short ribs, for example, are an ode to the dish that’s been on the menu since the restaurant opened its very first location in 2005.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. Sprinkle the short ribs with salt and pepper. In an ovenproof Dutch oven over medium-high heat, brown the ribs in oil in batches. Remove the meat and set it aside.

Add the celery, carrot and onion to the drippings, and cook them until they’re tender. Add the garlic, and cook for one minute longer. Add the wine and broth, stirring to loosen the browned bits from the pan.

Return the ribs to the pot. Add the parsley and thyme. Cover the pot and transfer it to the preheated oven. Cook the ribs for 2 hours to 2 hours and 30 minutes or until the meat is tender.

While the ribs are braising, in a small bowl, whisk all the butter ingredients until they’re blended. Transfer the mixture to a sheet of storage wrap, and roll it into a log. Refrigerate the butter until it’s chilled. Unwrap and slice it.

Place the hot mashed potatoes on a serving plate. Top them with the short ribs. Immediately top the ribs with a slice of Dijon butter and french-fried onions. Garnish the dish with additional fresh parsley, if desired.

Store any leftover short ribs in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Enjoy them within four days. Leftovers can be microwaved in a microwave-safe container, or they can be transferred to a Dutch oven and warmed in a 350° oven until they’re heated through.

Braised short ribs freeze like a dream. Store them in a freezer-safe airtight container and freeze them for three to four months. Defrost them completely in the refrigerator before warming them in the microwave or in the oven.

Short ribs are a heavily marbled cut of beef from the lower portion of the rib cage (the same area as the chuck and brisket). They have a robust, beefy flavor but contain a lot of connective tissue, so you need to cook them slowly with low heat for the meat to become tender.

Braising is one of the best (and most popular) ways to prepare short ribs. That said, you can make bone-in short ribs in a slow cooker or on a wood, pellet or charcoal smoker. To speed up the process, you can also make tender bone-in short ribs in a pressure cooker.

Cooper’s Hawk serves their short ribs with mashed potatoes and roasted vegetables, but that is far from the only pairing option. Serve them over a bowl of creamy polenta or on a bed of buttered egg noodles (similar to beef Stroganoff). For freshness, add a garden salad, grilled asparagus or creamed spinach for a more indulgent spin.

Sure! If you want to recreate Cooper’s Hawk braised short rib risotto, prepare this recipe as directed, minus the potatoes, veggies, and onion strings. Instead, saute a blend of mushrooms in a skillet and prepare this parmesan risotto while the short ribs braise in the oven. When everything is ready, shred the short ribs into small pieces and combine them with the mushrooms and risotto. Serve the risotto in shallow bowls with a few spoonfuls of braising liquid and a drizzle of white truffle oil.

#6579. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6578. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

The outer solar system will descend into chaos just a few billion years after the sun exhausts its fuel ‪—‬ much sooner than scientists previously thought, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the sun inevitably dies, not even the outer solar system will be safe from the resulting chaos, new research hints.Scientists have long thought the outer solar system ‪—‬ which comprises the four giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — would mostly retain its present-day appearance for hundreds of billions of years to come. But a new study suggests that the outer giants may develop weirdly shaped orbits as the sun runs out of fuel, causing the planets to cross paths and destroy themselves through collisions within three billion years of the sun's transformation into a red giant.

The findings, published Sept. 21 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could change our understanding of what kinds of exoplanets orbit certain stars.

In about 5 billion years, the sun will balloon outward as a red giant after exhausting all of the hydrogen in its core. During this red giant phase, our star will swell to 100 times its present-day size, gobbling up Mercury, Venus and possibly even Earth in the process, Nathan Kaib, a planetary scientist at the University of Oklahoma who wasn't involved in the new research, told Live Science in an email. Following this violent swelling, the sun will crumple into a collapsed core called a white dwarf.

Until now, scientists thought the four outer planets would escape this phase relatively unscathed. A 1998 simulation-based study suggested that the gas the sun spews from its outer layers will push this planetary quartet outward, doubling the radius of each planet's orbit. Only the gravitational impact of a runaway star could destabilize this new order, and such events are thought to occur only once every billion billion years.

These predictions hinged on the assumption that the sun will eject its outer layers smoothly. However, recent observations of stars suggest a jerkier loss of mass, with gas clouds lofted by plumes of plasma in the sun — as though our star were spitting out mass blobs. "They're kind of like coronal mass ejections, except much larger," Jim Fuller, a professor of theoretical astrophysics at Caltech and co-author of the new study, told Live Science in an email.

Each "blob" pushes the star backward, similar to how a fired bullet causes a gun to recoil. Although every push is small, moving the sun just a few feet per second, many pushes can, over time, impart the equivalent of an enormous kick that alters the sun's speed by several hundred feet per second. In fact, astronomers have already seen white dwarfs suffer such kicks in other star systems.

An illustration of the sun releasing a giant mass of plasma. As such large explosions increase in the sun's dying days, the recoil could disrupt the gravitational balance of the outer solar system.

When Fuller, who studied these kicks, described them to Konstantin Batygin, a professor of planetary science at Caltech and the study's first author, Batygin "realized this would have important consequences for the evolution of our own solar system," Fuller said. That's because the kicks change the sun's gravitational pulls on everything around it.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To determine how the sun's mass loss would influence the giant planets, Batygin created computer-based simulations of the sun and the outer planets. The researchers considered three scenarios: if the sun lost its mass smoothly, if it spit out distinct mass blobs during its entire time evolving as a red giant, and if the sun spewed the blobs only during its last stages. The researchers also varied each ejected blob's mass.

The first scenario produced results similar to those of previous studies, with the outer solar system retaining almost all of its features for billions of years. In contrast, the other two cases had drastically different results. Using 672 simulations, the researchers found that if the sun lost mass in blobs, the giant planets would be thrown into chaos, switching places, developing weirdly oval-shaped orbits, and even getting ejected out of the solar system entirely. Most dramatically, in 96% of the simulations with the heaviest ejected mass packets, the planets get destroyed as they crashed into each other.

These developments also happened much more rapidly — less than a few hundred million years after the sun transformed into a white dwarf, or even during the red giant phase, in the most extreme scenarios.

The study's findings hint that analogues of the present-day outer solar system around white dwarf stars are less likely to exist than previously thought. Kaib noted that the study's results suggest that planets with oval-shaped orbits should dominate instead. It's thought that habitable planets could exist around white dwarfs, but this study's findings show that our understanding of those distant star systems may be incomplete, and that such worlds may, in reality, be unstable.

Batygin, K., Fuller, J., & Adams, F. C. (2026). Terminal instability of the solar system triggered by stochastic solar mass loss. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1009(2), L22. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea290

#6576. Cranberry and Brie Stuffed Chicken

With its savory spinach filling, fruity sauce and gooey cheese topping, this cranberry Brie chicken makes any day a celebration.

Who doesn’t love a recipe that looks like it took hours in the kitchen, but is actually surprisingly easy to pull off? Our Test Kitchen’s cranberry Brie chicken is one of those impressive dinners. Tender chicken breasts are stuffed with a spinach filling, coated in bread crumbs and baked until golden. Then comes the best part: the cranberry sauce topping and slices of creamy Brie that melt right over the top.

With its festive colors and a blend of sweet and savory flavors, this dish is a great choice for Friendsgiving, Christmas Eve dinner or any occasion you want to impress guests. But don’t save it just for company! It’s also a fun way to dress up chicken breasts during the week.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a large skillet, cook the onion in oil until it’s almost tender. Add the spinach and garlic, and cook them until the spinach is wilted. Drain any liquid, if necessary. Season the filling with salt and pepper.

Pound the chicken breasts with a meat mallet to 1/4-inch thickness. Divide the spinach mixture among the pieces. Fold the chicken breasts in half, enclosing the filling, and secure them with toothpicks.

Place the bread crumbs and egg in separate shallow bowls. Dip the stuffed chicken breasts into the egg, then roll them in the crumbs to coat them. Place them seam side down in an 8-inch square baking dish coated with cooking spray. Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 25 minutes.

Spoon the cranberry sauce over the stuffed chicken breasts. Top them with slices of Brie (if desired, remove the rind from the Brie). Bake the chicken, uncovered, for 10 to 15 minutes longer or until a thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 165°. Discard the toothpicks before serving the chicken. If desired, garnish it with rosemary sprigs.

Let leftover cranberry Brie chicken cool slightly, then transfer it to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to four days. The breading will soften as it sits, especially under the cranberry sauce and melted Brie, but it’ll still be tasty once reheated.

Cranberry Brie chicken tastes best fresh out of the oven, but you can absolutely get a head start on prepping the recipe. Make the spinach filling, and stuff the chicken breasts, securing them with toothpicks. Cover and refrigerate both for up to 24 hours.

When you’re ready to make dinner, dip the chicken in the egg, coat it with bread crumbs and bake it as directed. Save the cranberry sauce and Brie for the last 10 to 15 minutes of baking. Waiting to coat the chicken until just before baking helps keep the bread crumbs from getting soggy.

Reheat cranberry Brie chicken, loosely covered with foil, in a 350° oven until it’s warmed through to 165°. The microwave also works for single servings, but the breading will be a little soggier.

We love Brie here because its mild flavor and creamy texture pair so well with the tart cranberry sauce, but it’s not your only option. Camembert has a similar creamy texture and earthy flavor, or you could use goat cheese if you want something bolder and tangier. For a milder, kid-friendly option, try mozzarella or fontina. Both melt beautifully into a gooey, cheesy topping.

Boneless skinless chicken thighs can work in this recipe, but their smaller size makes them a little trickier to pound thin and fold around the spinach filling. If possible, choose larger thighs, and use toothpicks to keep the filling tucked inside. Since thighs vary in size and thickness, you may need to adjust baking time. Use a meat thermometer to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165° before serving it.

Cranberry Brie chicken fits right in with holiday favorites like creamy mashed potatoes, roasted Brussels sprouts, stuffing or green bean casserole. For a more casual weeknight dinner, serve it over hot, fluffy rice to soak up the extra cranberry sauce, or pair it with roasted sweet potatoes or a simple green salad. And you can’t go wrong with a side of crusty bread, warm buttermilk biscuits or cornbread!

#6575. Dry Brushing: Why I Do It Every Day And All The Benefits

It seems like every time I watch a get-ready-with-me video, the first step of the routine is dry brushing. And while I’ve tried it here and there, I never found myself committing to the act. But this skin-care practice is beloved by not only the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow and Tracee Ellis Ross, but also by functional health doctors and medical professionals as well.

So what is dry brushing? It’s the act of running a bristled brush across your skin while working against gravity (so working toward your torso on limbs) to help with moving the body’s lymphatic system.

Everybody raves about the myriad of health benefits that comes along with dry brushing—from physically exfoliating your skin and eliminating strawberry skin to increasing blood flow and potentially diminishing the appearance of circulation.

Perhaps, then, it’s time to really give it a try.

True to its name, dry brushing involves running a bristled brush over dry skin, most commonly on the body (though occasionally, on the face if you’re working with a face-specific brush that’s much softer). “It is a powerful Ayurvedic practice that both exfoliates the skin and opens detox pathways to support lymphatic drainage and boost immunity,” says Lauren Berlingeri, co-founder of HigherDose.

A simple pre-shower ritual, it isn’t just used in Ayurvedic medicine to stimulate the skin and the body’s lymphatic system, but in traditional Chinese medicine (a.k.a. TCM) too. It’s a practice that has stood the test of time, which is always a good sign when trying to understand whether a wellness “trend” is really worth its salt.

As well as stimulating lymphatic drainage, which helps in detoxifying the body, dry brushing is supposed to be effective for removing dead skin cells to smooth skin, boosting blood circulation, and reducing puffiness and water retention. It is a great way to invigorate body and mind, especially at the start of the day. And some say it’s also great at reducing the appearance of cellulite, but from my personal research, this seems somewhat unfounded.

Sophie Bolvary, licensed massage therapist at Sanara, adds that the practice of dry brushing may boost our immune system: “The lymphatic system does not have a ‘pump’ of its own, meaning it only gets working when we start moving our body or when it is stimulated manually by dry brushing or light massage,” she explains.

She adds that different brushes can have a different effect on the body. Dry brushes made with boar-hair bristles are ideal for daily use and exfoliation. Dry brushes with ionic-copper bristles carry the added benefit of sweeping your body in negative ions, which is known for antiviral and antibacterial properties in traditional medicine. It also may bring us full body-mind refreshment as an added self-care benefit.

“The brisk rhythmic motion creates a sensory reset that I find both grounding and energizing,” Bolvary adds. “Helping to sharpen mental alertness and brighten my mood.” Pro tip: Sprinkle an essential-oil blend (like something with citrus) to your dry brush to further wake up your senses.

I’ve used a dry body brush during episodic health kicks previously, but rarely consistently—but my coworker swears by it before every shower, especially when she’s taking an “Everything Shower.” What I’ve most noticed since making it (at least) a four-times-a-week thing is that my skin is infinitely looking more polished and brighter. It’s an excellent way to quickly slough off the dead skin cells that form a grey veil over what was months before a summer tan, and it’s certainly a good way to wake yourself up in the morning.

I have found that combining it with a “contrast” shower—i.e., turning the temperature hot, then cold, then hot, then cold—makes me feel extremely energized, particularly after a vigorous workout. You also don’t really need to commit to doing five minutes to reap the benefits—give it three minutes and you’ll feel fantastic as you start your day. It’s worth noting that—as hard as I willed it—dry brushing won’t stimulate lymphatic drainage enough to cure a hangover. This is deeply disappointing, but I continue to search for a fix.

Newbies to the practice should know that once you’ve dry-brushed, you’ll likely experience an itchy, tingling sensation, along with some possible redness, which soon settles. This feeling quickly becomes less prominent with regular use, but it’s actually a sign that your circulation is revved up and blood is en route to the surface of the skin.

You also might feel, for lack of a better way to phrase it, like your skin is dusty. This is all the dead skin cells you just exfoliated off—which is why most people prefer to do this practice before hopping in the shower. Don’t fret, a little big of your favorite body soap will take care of it.

Dry body brushing is a really easy—and affordable—ritual to commit to, which is why it gets a yes from me. You can’t always see the many benefits it has on the body, but you can often feel them. I have personally noticed a more even skin tone, slightly lighter-feeling legs (not yet as streamlined as Paltrow’s, unfortunately), and more morning vitality. I also firmly believe that taking a few intentional minutes to do something positive for your well-being each day is underrated.

Next up… time to crack body moisturizing. A look at the dry brushes we’d recommend, below.

There are a few negative side effects that can occur if you’re not careful. Marisa Garshick, MD, board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology, says that it may cause irritation or micro-tears in the skin if too much pressure is applied. You’ll also want to consider what skin conditions you might be dealing with and if your skin type can tolerate all this brushing. Dr. Garshick says it’s not recommended for anyone with sensitive, broken, or inflamed skin like eczema or psoriasis.

Bolvary adds that you’ll want to be mindful about cleaning your brush (more on how to do that later). Because of the exfoliating nature of dry brushing, there could be a lot of skin-shedding debris that builds up in the brush that can make dry brushing ineffective or irritate your skin further.

Dr. Garshick says that dry brushing can be done one to two times a week if you have sensitive skin, as frequent brushing might cause irritation. But if your skin can tolerate it, Bolvary says that it can be a daily practice. She recommends doing it at the start of your day, right before hopping in the shower. “Some people find it more stimulating and energizing than a cup of coffee,” she says. Here’s to hoping.

Dry brushing done by a professional will give you a more in-depth treatment. “The practitioner takes care of the work, and reaches all the hard-to-reach areas, while you simply enjoy the awakening sensations,” says Bolvary. “Also, the practitioner can demonstrate proper technique and pressure for your skin and body type.”

But that doesn’t mean doing it at home won’t have its own benefits. She says it’s helpful to look at a lymphatic glow map: “A very easy Google search, which can outline the general flow of lymph and how to sweep into the main lymph ports of the body.” After a few tries on your own, she says, you get used to it.

Bolvary says that because dry brushes are usually made with natural materials, it’s best to use natural, non-chemical cleaning solutions to clean your brushes. “I like to get a bowl of warm water with several drops of tea tree oil and place the brush bristles down to let it soak for about 30 minutes. Then set it aside to dry.”

But keep in mind that your brush will soften over time and will eventually shed a little with regular washing. “These tools are not meant to last forever,” she says. “So if your brush has become too soft and the bristles are falling out with every use, it may be time for a new one.”

Try to wash your brush once every two weeks and spritz it with something like tea tree mist after every use. Bolvary also recommends leaving it in a window to air-dry rather than on your shower ledge, where it can easily get dirty.

#6574. This Genius Trick Makes Perfectly Portioned Cinnamon Rolls—No Ruler or Guessing Required

This clever little move turns your knife into a measuring guide for cinnamon rolls.

I have no objection to a shortcut in the kitchen. I’m happy to let boxed cake mix handle dessert or a great jar of pasta sauce get dinner moving. But I just can’t make peace with cinnamon rolls from a can. I want to love them. I appreciate the convenience, and I understand the appeal of having warm cinnamon rolls before the coffee is finished brewing. They just never quite satisfy that craving for a warm, deliciously gooey cinnamon roll.

Some viral upgrades make a compelling case—particularly the heavy cream bath and generous additions of butter and brown sugar. But my long-standing love for cinnamon rolls has much more to do with the soft, pillowy dough, so I’m willing to wait through a rise or two.

Having committed to that, though, I’m still interested in anything that makes the process easier. So when I saw a video of someone flipping a knife over a log of cinnamon roll dough to mark perfectly even portions, I wanted to try it. Cutting equal slices by eye can involve a surprising amount of second-guessing when you’d really just like to get them in the pan. I made our classic cinnamon roll recipe and put the trick to the test.

The clever part of this trick is that the knife becomes its own measurement. Rather than judging the thickness of each slice, you use the width of the blade to mark equal portions along the dough roll before slicing it into pieces.

Once your dough is filled and rolled into a log, gently lay the blade flat across the top at one end, with the knife running crosswise over the log. Then flip it onto its opposite flat side, moving along the dough one blade-width at a time. It looks a little like the knife is doing small somersaults, with its edge leaving a light indentation at each turn.

Continue down the log, using just enough pressure to leave visible marks. Then go back and slice through the dough at those marks.

This worked beautifully with our classic cinnamon rolls, but the same technique would work with just about any cinnamon roll recipe. The turning motion was simple, and the knife left an evenly spaced cutting guide along the dough. Once the marks were there, I could slice the rolls without measuring each one or estimating where the next cut should go.

I particularly liked being able to see all the portions before I started cutting. It made the job feel settled: The spacing was already worked out, and all I had to do was follow it. For something that takes so little effort, it’s a useful bit of precision.

This is the kind of cinnamon roll shortcut I can get behind. I still get the homemade rolls I wanted, but there’s one less thing to fuss over before the pan goes into the oven.

#6572. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming — in which the dreamer is aware that they are dreaming and can sometimes influence the dream's trajectory — is a skill that can be honed, a new study finds. And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month.

The study's results could have practical benefits, said Daniel Morris, a cognitive neuroscientist at Northwestern University who studies dreams and was not involved with the work. "Lucid dreaming can benefit people with nightmares by allowing them to transform their nightmares into positive dreams and feel greater agency in their dreams," Morris told Live Science in an email.

Before this study, published Sept. 28 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, neuroscientists tried to induce lucid dreaming with various methods. These included meditation exercises and so-called reality checks, in which participants ask themselves while awake whether unusual phenomena they encounter — such as people wearing odd Halloween costumes — are real or if they're dreaming. The idea is that they will ask themselves the same question in their sleep during bizarre dreams.

However, "for most people, our day-to-day lives may not feel 'dream-like,'" Morris said, explaining why reality checks have had mixed results and don't reliably trigger lucid dreaming.

Since dream-like scenarios are rare in waking life, the neuroscientists behind the new study used VR simulations of bizarre situations to complement reality-check exercises.

The team, based at the University of Trento in Italy, recruited university students and asked them to meditate and then perform the VR training. The meditation was intended to increase students' awareness of what they were thinking about in a given moment. Each time they encountered bizarre happenings in the VR environment, such as objects or people violating laws of physics or rapid switches from one scene to another, they performed reality checks.

After the training, participants went home and were asked to keep a dream diary that they wrote in every morning. They also filled out daily questionnaires, citing the number of dreams they recalled and how many they remembered being lucid.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The participants experienced lucid dreams four times more often than participants did in a second group that did reality checks without performing any meditation or VR training. The study also included another comparison group, in which participants carried out reality checks during realistic rather than dream-like VR simulations; these participants were over eight times less likely to report lucid dreams. This latter comparison ensured that the results were not caused solely by the use of VR, the researchers said.

When participants encountered something strange, like branches covering a door, they actively asked themselves whether it was real.

It was particularly surprising to find that such little training with the dream-like VR simulations was needed to develop lucid dreaming as a skill, said study co-author Nicola De Pisapia, a neuroscientist at the University of Trento. His team ran the experiment for only a month because any longer would have been too demanding for the participants, De Pisapia noted.

Study co-author Andrea Signorelli, a doctoral student in De Pisapia's lab, thinks the VR intervention is at the heart of why the approach worked. People often don't realize that they're dreaming because the dreams "fool" your senses and feel realistic in the moment, he explained.

"Virtual reality is the technology to fool you on stereoscopic vision and auditory information," he said. The term "stereoscopic" refers to techniques that create 3D illusions from 2D images by mimicking how human eyes see.

"It's basically the most immersive technology that we have at the moment," making it a good intervention for reality check exercises, Signorelli said.

The team also compared the number of lucid dreams participants reported against their total number of recalled dreams, which revealed an interesting pattern. On average, participants in each group recalled more dreams after starting the experiment than they did beforehand. However, the dream-simulating VR group recalled the fewest dreams overall after entering the experiment, even though they had the highest number of lucid dreams.

Signorelli speculated that perhaps it takes a lot of energy to have lucid dreams, which could divert resources away from recalling other dreams. Morris argued that, alternatively, participants in the lucid-dream VR group "may have been less motivated to report non-lucid dreams than the control groups." So there may have been some bias in the reporting.

The study had some limitations, such as its small sample size of 38 participants. Plus, neither of the two control groups were asked to meditate, so it is impossible to say whether the meditations or the dreamlike VR sessions had more influence over lucid dreaming in the test group.

The team is now doing a follow-up study in which the meditation part has been removed, Signorelli said, to reveal whether the VR dream scenarios are the critical factor, as suspected.

Signorelli said that he would like to see lucid-dream training tailored for each individual. For example, the VR simulations could be personalized to simulate a recurrent nightmare that a given person experiences, training them to recognize triggers specific to that dream, he said.

"Other future research could explore the potential therapeutic benefits of this intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety, or PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]," Morris suggested.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6570. The 10 Best Aldi Finds of November Include the Cutest Stocking Stuffer for Little Shoppers

From flavor mash-up snacks and holiday decor to a very special Barbie doll, these November Aldi Finds deserve a spot in your shopping cart.

November is one of my favorite months to go grocery shopping. First, no one can deny that it is peak soup season, so I love stocking up on ingredients for creamy butternut squash soup or a classic lentil stew. I never seem to mind that the sun sets earlier when I have a truly cozy lineup of fall dinner recipes.

And of course, Thanksgiving preparations take up a bulk of the month as well. In my family, I am tasked with two things: bread and Thanksgiving desserts. This year I am going to try my hand at making a sourdough pecan pie! Aldi is definitely the first place I go for my Thanksgiving shopping, because it’s guaranteed to have all my ingredients in stock. And, of course, there’s no shortage of seasonal goodies to look forward to.

Every month, Aldi drops a slew of new items and brings back some customer favorites. Since the grocery store is famous for its motto of “Here today, gone tomorrow,” I’ve turned my passion into an inside scoop so you can stock up while things last. Here are the most exciting November Aldi Finds that will make the holiday season even better.

Nothing says “welcome to the holidays” quite like a big wreath on the front door. This wreath has tiny pine cones and lights, which makes it even more magical. I love that it’s available with either a red or green velvet ribbon, so you can choose which suits your personal aesthetic best.

Of course, if you prefer savory treats over sweet ones, then you might really enjoy these turkey stuffing-flavored potato chips. All the classic Thanksgiving flavors you love, but in chip form. The wavy chip makes it perfect for dipping—say, in some homemade cranberry sauce?

This board is such a great idea! The snowman outline gives you plenty of opportunities to arrange your favorite meats and cheeses in a cute way. The snap-top lid ensures everything stays in place during transit from your house to wherever the party is. It’s so festive, I might just be giving these as gifts this year.

I’m a sucker for any kind of fancy bread, and this loaf in particular caught my eye. Imagine the pillowy sweet softness of a classic brioche, but with added maple nut flavor. It sounds like a breakfast dream come true! I’ll be using this for Thanksgiving leftover sandwiches and French toast.

If there’s one thing Aldi does well, it’s providing exceptionally budget-friendly dupes of much fancier brands. Like this adorable cherry red braiser pan, which has a leaf design on the lid. It might cost upward of $300 from some brands, but Aldi gives it to you at a mere fraction of the price.

OK, this is so cool! A special Aldi-branded Barbie doll is a perfect stocking stuffer for any of the grocery-obsessed kids (or adults!) in your life. This Barbie comes with her own shopping cart and reusable tote, so she is ready to stock up on all her favorite Aldi finds.

I have several holiday runners from Aldi, and they are some of my favorite pieces of decor. This beautiful floral version has big poinsettia flowers and holly leaves, so it’s sure to make a statement on your table for the holidays. It’s machine washable, too, which is very convenient—you don’t need to stress if someone spills red wine on it (speaking from experience!)

This has been my absolute favorite seasonal Aldi find over the last few years. Adding a few of these fancy flavored marshmallows to a simple cup of hot cocoa transforms it into an irresistible treat. I am partial to the peppermint flavor, but the salted caramel marshmallows are also incredible. And again, they are perfect for gifting!

Which Aldi Find are you most excited for this month? Let us know in the comments below!

#6568. This Coffee Subscription Delivers Some of the Freshest Beans We’ve Tried

It's one of the best gifts you can give to coffee lovers this holiday season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It really doesn't get fresher than this. A Storyville coffee subscription delivers delicious beans right to your doorstep.

We’ve all been there. Standing in the grocery store staring at dozens of coffee brands and trying to decide which one might perk us up, only to end up scowling at a subpar cup of sludge the next morning. Well, those days are over because Storyville, one of Seattle’s best coffee shops, now delivers freshly roasted beans straight to your door.

I tried a Storyville coffee subscription, and I assure you that you’ll never have to waste your time (or money) on stale beans again. Here’s everything you need to know about this caffeinated club.

Storyville is one of the highest-rated coffee shops in Seattle, with locations at Pike Place and at 1st and Madison. They also have a roasting studio you can tour to see exactly where your coffee beans are roasted before making their way to your door. But if you can’t make it to Seattle, they also offer coffee subscription services with nationwide shipping.

The brand sources premium-grade green coffees and roasts each bean varietal individually before blending. Beans are roasted on the darker end of medium and feature a rich, natural sweetness with notes of chocolate and caramel. Unlike many other dark roasts, this coffee has a smooth finish and no bitterness. Best of all, Storyville ships its coffee immediately after roasting.

Storyville subscriptions are highly customizable in order to fit your needs. First, choose between whole beans and single-serve pods. Then choose the quantity and delivery frequency that best suits your needs. You can pause, skip or cancel via text at any time. Moreover, you’ll receive 20% off, among other perks.

I am a coffee fiend. On any given day, I’m three cups in by 9 a.m. That’s why I couldn’t wait to get my hands on a bag of real Seattle coffee.

My order arrived on Wednesday, October 28. I received a bag of Prologue coffee beans, Sunrise espresso beans and Epilogue decaf coffee beans. I knew the roast dates would be stamped on the bags, but I was amazed to see that my beans had been roasted just days prior, on October 25 and October 27. Talk about fresh!

I opened the Prologue first and poured the entire bag into the bean hopper of my De’Longhi Rivelia. After brewing, I took a sip before adding my cream and sugar and was amazed by how smooth it was. It was fresh and flavorful without a hint of bitterness. I love a dark roast and could drink this all day long.

The next day, I opened the Sunrise espresso beans. I used it to make a regular cup of coffee followed by an Americano. Like the Prologue, the beans were clearly fresh, and the coffee was exceptionally smooth! I’ll be saving this bag along with the decaf for espresso martinis with my girlfriends.

As a dark roast gal, I’ve had my fair share of coffee that tastes bitter or burnt. I didn’t get any notes of bitterness from Storyville coffee. I’ll also point out that a bag of Prologue coffee lasted one week. Given how much coffee I drink plus the fact that my husband tends to make a cup here and there, I’m not surprised we went through it so quickly. Luckily, the subscription is completely customizable. If you drink as much coffee as I do, you’ll want to order two or three bags at a time. But if you just enjoy one cup per day, then one bag at a time will suffice.

That said, these beans are so fresh we wouldn’t be surprised if you start drinking more coffee than usual. And we certainly wouldn’t blame you!

It’s also easy to send a subscription as a gift. Simply head over to their gifting page and opt for three, five, eight or 12 prepaid shipments.

#6567. These Wine Glasses Are the Only Ones That Can Survive My Clumsiness

I spent years living with roommates and making due with our collective assortment of mismatched dishware, throwing washed take-out containers haphazardly into a cupboard and reusing them until they were cracked and stained, and living with a pantry that was in a constant state of moderate disarray. But when I moved in with my boyfriend, I took the opportunity to get my shit together. I pride myself on being a relatively put-together person, and that now translates to my kitchen too. I’ve got a cabinet full of well-organized food storage containers with their corresponding lids, I keep my spices neatly stacked in deli containers with labeled with color-coded kitchen tape, I replaced my chipped water glasses with a matching set, and I have a special drawer that houses the linens, taper candles, and flatware I pull out when I’m hosting. It all feels very adult.

Until recently, though, there was one remaining aspect of my kitchen that still needed help. While I have more fun coupes and rocks glasses than I know what to do with, I haven’t owned a matching set of wine glasses since college—in fact, at the time of my move, I had two left to my name. It’s not for lack of trying: I’ve tested out glassware during my time at BA, bringing home countless options in the hopes that they’d be my forever stems. I’ve somehow managed to break every single one of them, which has become a running joke for those that know me.

But despite my clumsiness, I’m not willing to sacrifice style for durability. I want a thin-stemmed, thin-rimmed, elegant wine glass that won’t snap in two the minute I lay my hands on it. Is that too much to ask?

For the longest time, I thought it might be, and had resigned myself to sipping wine out of stemless tumblers—until I discovered Gabriel-Glas’s StandArt All Purpose Wine Glass. They’ve got a sleek, slightly conical shape that I find enhances reds, whites, and rosés alike, with a slight curve between the bowl and the rim that adds a touch of personality to an otherwise classic silhouette. The stem is thin enough to satisfy my desire for elegance without being so delicate that I’m scared I’ll snap it, and the laser-cut rim is a joy to sip from.

Because the glasses are machine-blown from a single piece of molten crystal, they have none of the weak points that tend to form where traditional multipart glasses are joined. The machine-blown construction also keeps the cost per glass low enough that I won’t mind replacing one if (let’s be real, when) I do drop and shatter it. But I’m pleased to report that as of right now, all six of my beloved StandArt glasses are intact and ready to take on my new apartment’s first season of holiday hosting and cozy weather hangs. Bring on the winter reds and festive bottles of bubbly.

It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.

But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.

"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."

The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.

This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.

For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees ‪—‬ such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England ‪—‬ also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.

But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.

A microscopic image of skin cells from the dogfish shark.

"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.

Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.

These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.

Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.

There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.

"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

#6565. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6564. This Old-School Drink Is Making a Comeback for the Coziest Winter Cocktails

Port isn't just for sipping after dinner. We asked a respected winemaker about how this rich, fruity wine can be used to make easy winter cocktails.

For my birthday, a friend gifted me a bottle of Angel’s Envy bourbon. It was a fantastic gift (thank you, Jaclyn!), but what stood out to me was a detail on the label: “finished in port wine barrels.”

Usually I hear of bourbon barrels being used to age other things. The Goose Island Bourbon County Stout, for example, is a beer that’s aged in bourbon barrels, and it’s so special that people will line up outside grocery stores in the hope of grabbing a pack. But I’m less familiar with port wine, and I wanted to learn more.

I’ve been seeing port pop up on menus and in cocktail recipes with more frequency. When I think of port, I imagine the nobility in medieval times sipping from big pewter goblets. Of course, you don’t need to be a royal to enjoy it!

I reached out to an expert for some advice on how to incorporate port into more of my winter cocktails. He gave me a crash course in everything I needed to know about the wine, and shared some of the best ways to use it in cocktails.

I connected with David Guimaraens, head winemaker for Taylor Fladgate. Born in Portugal, David is the sixth generation of his family to be involved in the port business. He’s widely recognized as one of the most gifted winemakers in the modern port industry, and his tips on how to winterize cocktails with port are simple enough to incorporate into any cocktail routine.

Taste of Home: For someone who may be unfamiliar with the category, how would you explain what port is and what distinguishes it from other styles of wine?

David Guimaraens: Port is a fortified wine produced in Portugal’s Douro Valley, one of the world’s oldest demarcated wine regions. What sets it apart is that a small amount of grape spirit is added during fermentation. This stops the fermentation process so some of the natural sweetness from the grapes remains in the finished product. The result is a uniquely rich, concentrated fruit wine with an incredible depth of flavor.

There are many different styles of port, from fresh, vibrant ruby ports to complex, aged tawnies and exceptional vintage ports. That diversity makes port a far more versatile category than many people realize, with styles suited to everything from cocktails and aperitifs to food pairings and after-dinner enjoyment.

TOH: What qualities does port bring to a mixed drink, and why does it work particularly well as a cocktail ingredient?

DG: Port brings fruit notes, sweetness and complexity to a cocktail. Depending on the style, its flavor profile can range from fresh berry and spice to dried fruit, nuts and caramel. It is remarkably versatile behind the bar. Port can replace or complement vermouth and other sweet components in classic cocktails. Its concentration of flavor allows you to add complexity to a drink without a long list of ingredients.

TOH: Why is port trending for winter cocktails and seasonal entertaining?

DG: There is something naturally comforting about port during the colder months. Its fruit and spice notes pair particularly well with seasonal flavors such as cranberry, orange, cinnamon, ginger and chocolate, making it a versatile choice for holiday entertaining. Port has also always been a wine for sharing. Serving it in a cocktail or a simple spritz offers a more informal, contemporary way to enjoy that tradition and bring port to the table.

TOH: For someone experimenting with port cocktails at home for the first time, what is the easiest way to begin? Are there simple serves, ratios or ingredient pairings you recommend?

DG: Keep it simple. You don’t need to be a mixologist to make a great port cocktail. A port spritz is an easy place to start: Serve port over plenty of ice, top with sparkling water or tonic, and finish with a slice or twist of fresh citrus. It is refreshing, simple to prepare and easy to adapt to your own taste.

TOH: For consumers shopping for port to use in cocktails, what should they look for when selecting a bottle? Does someone need to invest in an expensive Port to make a great cocktail?

DG: Absolutely not. In fact, I would reserve great vintage ports for enjoying on their own!

For cocktails, look for a good-quality, fruit-driven reserve ruby port with enough character to stand up alongside the other ingredients. Fonseca Bin 27 is a great example: It is approachable and full of rich berry fruit, and it has the structure and depth to work extremely well in cocktails.

Have you made port cocktails before? Let us know your favorite version in the comments below!

#6562. Spiced and Glazed Roast Turkey

Our mission: A roast turkey that’s boldly spiced, beautifully glazed, and—can we type this loudly enough?—PROPERLY COOKED. That means juicy breast meat, tender dark meat, and plenty of deeply browned skin. Andy Baraghani and Brad Leone’s solution? Break the bird into five pieces: two wings, two legs, and one whole breast. Roasting the bird in parts gives you more control over when each piece is done—no dry breast meat or tough legs.

They didn’t slouch on flavor either. A peppery dry brine with garlic powder, onion powder, and smoked paprika gets to work 24–48 hours before the turkey goes into the oven. Then comes the glaze: a savory-tangy mix of soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, orange zest, and herbs. Brushed onto the turkey as it roasts, it builds a glossy, deeply burnished finish. And because the pieces cook on a wire rack set inside a baking sheet, you get more exposed skin for browning and a more even cook overall.

If the idea of doing surgery on a raw turkey gives you a stress rash, ask your butcher to do it—even at the supermarket. Request a 12–14-lb. turkey cut into five pieces, with the thighs attached to the drumsticks, the breast left whole, and the backbone removed. If they ask why, just say: Yes, you’re making that ridiculous Bon Appétit recipe. If you’d rather do the honors yourself, here’s our guide to breaking down a whole turkey.

Choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. Many supermarket birds are already treated with a salt solution, sometimes labeled “self-basting,” “enhanced,” or “contains a solution.” Adding this dry brine on top can make the turkey overly salty. Check the packaging before you buy.

Should I rinse off the dry brine before roasting?

No. Leave the seasoning on the turkey when you coat it with oil. Some of the spice mixture may rub off, but that’s fine. There’s no need to rinse the bird, and washing raw poultry can spread bacteria around your kitchen.

Can I use the pan drippings to make gravy?

Yes, but taste them first. Between the seasoned dry brine and soy-based glaze, the drippings can be quite salty and intensely flavored. Use them sparingly and taste your gravy before adding more salt. For a simpler option, try our Make-Ahead Gravy, which doesn’t require drippings at all.

Read our guide to turkey cooking times, no matter the bird’s size or your preferred cooking method.

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 24 hours dry-brining

Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck and giblets removed, breast side up, on a cutting board and pat dry. Grip a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate the wing from the breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get into the place where the joint meets the socket). Remove wing; repeat on the other side.

Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until the ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through the joint to separate leg. Repeat on the other side.

Now for the breast: Position the turkey breast side down with the opening facing you. Using kitchen shears, cut along one side of backbone until you get all the way through the neck end, then turn the turkey 180° and cut through the other side to remove the backbone (save it for making stock).

Very finely grind 2 Tbsp. whole black peppercorns and 2 Tbsp. whole pink or black peppercorns in a spice mill or mortar and pestle; transfer to a medium bowl. Add ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. garlic powder, 2 Tbsp. onion powder, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1 Tbsp. smoked paprika, and use your fingers to mix together.

Place turkey pieces, skin side up, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. Sprinkle salt mixture liberally all over turkey, patting to adhere. You may not need all of it, but it’s good to have extra since some will end up on the baking sheet. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 24 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil to make cleanup easy and set rack back inside. Arrange turkey pieces on rack, skin side up, and let sit at room temperature up to 2 hours to help decrease the cooking time.

Meanwhile, cook small handful of hardy herbs (such as sage, rosemary, bay leaves, and/or thyme), 4 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, ⅓ cup low-sodium soy sauce, ⅓ cup (packed; 71 g) light brown sugar, and ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until sugar is dissolved and glaze thickens slightly (it should just barely coat a spoon), 10–12 minutes. Remove glaze from heat.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Rub turkey with 6 Tbsp. neutral oil (such as vegetable, peanut, or canola) and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet. Roast turkey, rotating baking sheet halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown, 20–25 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 20 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast registers 150°, and 170° when inserted into the thickest part of the thighs, 50–70 minutes longer (total cooking time will be 1–1½ hours). Skin should be deep golden brown and shiny. Transfer turkey to a cutting board; tent loosely with foil. Let rest 30–60 minutes before carving.

Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published in our November 2019 issue. We’ve updated the introduction with additional cooking guidance and answers to common reader questions; we’ve also updated the recipe for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving recipes →

#6561. Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies Treats

Recipe by Cori Cooper, flagstaff, Arizona

Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats are party-ready, from the bright rainbow colors and fruity flavor to the crisp, chewy texture and marshmallow pull.

If there are Rice Krispies treats on any table full of treats, I’ll make a beeline for them before even glancing at brownies or cupcakes. The combination of light, crisp cereal and chewy marshmallow hits every time. There will always be a place in my heart for the classic ones, but playing around with different Rice Krispies treats variations brings me endless joy. Cori Cooper, a Community Cook from Flagstaff, Arizona, feels the same way, which led her to create these colorful Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats.

By just switching to a rainbow-colored, fruity cereal, Cori transformed the dessert without changing the beloved texture of the original or making it too sweet. I’ll be making these for my next bake sale. Hopefully they make it out of my kitchen!

Place the cereal and half of one package of mini marshmallows in a large bowl.

In a microwave-safe bowl or a large saucepan over low heat, melt the remaining marshmallows in butter, stirring until they’re smooth. Stir in the salt, if using it, then remove the mixture from the heat. Pour it over the cereal mixture.

Editor’s Tip: If using the microwave, heat the butter and marshmallows in 30- to 45-second intervals, stirring in between, to prevent the butter from getting too hot and splattering.

Press into a lightly greased 8-inch square baking pan using waxed paper or a lightly greased spatula. Let the mixture cool to room temperature. Cut it into bars.

Editor’s Tip: For bars that hold together but still have an airy bite and chewy texture, press the cereal mixture evenly into the pan, but don’t use all your might and pack them in.

Store Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats at room temperature, tightly wrapped, for three to five days. Technically, they last longer, but the cereal will start to get stale and the treats will become brittle over time. You can leave the treats in the baking pan and tightly wrap the entire pan, or transfer cut squares to an airtight food storage container, adding a piece of parchment between layers to keep them from sticking together.

You can freeze Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats for up to six weeks, but they won’t have the same soft, stretchy texture as freshly made treats. Pack the treats in a freezer-proof food storage bag, pressing out the excess air, or place them in a container with an airtight lid, adding a piece of parchment between the layers. They will thaw quickly, so just let them stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes before eating them.

Cereal treats can end up hard instead of soft, stretchy and chewy if the marshmallows are stale or overheated, or if you pack the treats too tightly into the baking dish. Stale marshmallows don’t have the same moisture and bounce as fresh ones, making them tough from the start. And since marshmallows are mostly sugar, they can burn or become candy-like if overcooked, which makes the treats unpleasantly firm. If you compress the cereal too much, you crush out all its air, which results in dense treats that are hard to bite through.

You can use several different pans for these Fruity Pebbles Rice Krispies treats to vary their shape or thickness. For thinner treats, press the cereal mixture into a 9-inch square baking pan. For a different shape, use an 8-inch or 9-inch round cake pan and then cut the cereal treats into triangles, like slices of pie.

Since these are Fruity Pebbles treats, you should keep at least half the amount of Fruity Pebbles, but if you’re a few cups short (this happens to me all the time), you can make up the difference with one of the best childhood cereals, like Cheerios or Lucky Charms. You can use almost any crisp, puffed or flaked cereal, but consider what will taste the best with the fruity base. I’d recommend a cereal with light sweetness and a nutty or vanilla flavor so you don’t overshadow the Fruity Pebbles.
