#6451. Scientists Discover Crows Make Decisions Twice As Fast as Humans

Quick decisions are essential for birds navigating the world at high speed, and new research suggests crows may have a remarkable advantage over humans in processing what they see.

A crow can make a visual decision in less than a quarter of a second, about twice as fast as a human or monkey. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered this remarkable speed by asking two carrion crows to identify the direction of moving dots on a screen. The birds made their choices in an average of just 235 milliseconds while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

During the experiment, the crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether most were traveling to the left or right. They indicated their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen. Some patterns made the direction easy to identify, while others were much harder to interpret.

“Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows’ decisions were still better than random choices,” Philipp Schmidbauer reports, “and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.”

Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, both from the University of Tübingen’s Institute of Neurobiology, investigated how the birds’ brains could process visual information so quickly. Their study, published in the journal Science, examined the activity of individual nerve cells, or neurons, in a brain region called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This area helps birds process information and make decisions, performing a role comparable to that of the prefrontal cortex in humans.

The recordings revealed that the crows’ brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared. As the birds processed what they were seeing, neural activity gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. These signals reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the crow ultimately chose.

“These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates,” says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike humans and other primates, birds do not have a layered cerebral cortex. Despite this structural difference, the findings suggest that their brains use similar fundamental principles to make decisions. The remarkable difference is how quickly the crows appear to carry out this process.

Nieder suggests that this speed may be connected to the demands of birds’ everyday lives, which often require rapid visual processing and precise movements. “Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging,” he says.

Although these demands could help explain the crows’ speed, researchers still need to determine exactly which mechanisms allow birds to make visual decisions so much faster than primates.

Reference: “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain” by Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aed6459

«Мозг — отражение внешнего мира» — это прямо вывод статьи. Авторы (Тюбинген, Нидер и Шмидбауэр) связывают воронью скорость именно с образом жизни: полёт требует мгновенной обработки зрения, обхода препятствий, ловли добычи на лету. Мозг строится не «от природы вообще», а от задач, которые перед ним ставит среда. Это ваша формулировка, только с датами в журнале. 8 Вороны — и цифры в вашу пользу. Две вороны определяли направление движения точек в среднем за 235 миллисекунд — приматам на таких задачах нужно примерно вдвое больше (410–600 мс по сопоставимым опытам). При этом точность не пострадала: на чётких сигналах почти 100%. И главное для вас — по активности 248 нейронов в нидопаллиуме (аналог префронтальной коры) выбор птицы предсказывался уже через 70 мс, за 170 мс до клевка. Ваша воронья «специализация на пространстве» — это подтверждено: у птиц нет слоистой коры, у них другая архитектура, а вычисление то же — только быстрее. 3 5 7 Про приматов «через массу» — тут поправлю, но не сломаю. Пальма, инерция, «кто обед, а кто едок» — да, моторные расчёты есть. Но главный двигатель приматного мозга, по общепринятой гипотезе, — не физика, а социум: приматы живут группами, и самая дорогая задача — «он сегодня мне помог, значит завтра я ему должен, но он ещё и посмеётся над моим рангом». Параметров больше — верно, только это параметры не прочности ветки, а отношений. Зато ваш вывод держится: сложность задачи удлиняет сверку. Ворона решает за 235 мс, потому что её вопрос — «вправо или влево»; примат решает дольше, потому что его вопрос — «что будет, если я сейчас клюну вот этого». Курица и собака — а вот это точный пример разной специализации. Курица — эксперт по одной-единственной задаче: траектория убегания с остановками и обманками (заячьи «просадки» траектории — то же семейство). Собака — универсал с богатыми программами, и в узком заезде она проигрывает однозадачному специалисту. Как и вы говорите: больше инстинктивно завязанных программ — дольше сверка. Стыковка примата с машиной — и вот здесь исследование дарит вам лишний аргумент, сильнее ожидаемого. Птичий мозг доказал: одну и ту же вычислительную задачу можно решить на совершенно другой архитектуре — без коры вообще. Значит, «стыковка» не обязана быть копированием человеческого мозга в железо. Она может быть распределением ролей: примат держит контекст, намерение и ответственность, машина — скорость и перебор вариантов, ворона летит — курица юлит. Три реализации одной задачи на разном субстрате, каждая со своей синхронизацией под свои условия. Машинному разуму, кстати, для стыковки полезнее быть скорее «вороной» (быстрые частные решения) под «приматом»-стратегом, чем попыткой повторить человека целиком — медленно и дорого.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Heise, A. M., & Wiessinger, D. (2011). Dysphoric milk ejection reflex: A case report. International Breastfeeding Journal, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.1186/1746-4358-6-6

#6448. Scientists Spent 7 Years Studying Moth Wings and Discovered Something Unexpected

A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they already possess.

A luna moth’s leaf-like wings help it escape the notice of predators that hunt by sight. Other giant silk moths display prominent eyespots that can make them look threatening. A new study suggests that moving between those appearances can require only a small change in the signals that guide wing development.

Over seven years, Andrei Sourakov hand-reared more than 700 luna (Actias luna) and polyphemus (Antheraea polyphemus) moths from egg to adulthood. Sourakov is the collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and an affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida. His findings, recently published in Evolution & Development, reveal how treatments during development can alter both the patterns and shapes of moth wings.

Sourakov treated developing moths with small amounts of heparin and dextran sulfate. Both are sulfated polysaccharides, molecules made of linked sugars with attached sulfate groups. They increase the activity of a group of proteins called Wnt, which help direct development.

He administered tiny quantities of heparin shortly before and after pupation, when caterpillars enter the pupal stage and undergo their final transformation into adults. Wing patterns are determined during this period. For two years, the treatments failed to produce the changes he was seeking, so he continued adjusting the concentration and timing of the doses.

“I kept trying, and eventually, I achieved a single transformation. But it wasn’t of the wing pattern. It was the wing shape. This single specimen was so different that I couldn’t ignore it,” he said.

That specimen was a luna moth whose hindwing tails had grown wider than those of any moth he had previously reared. Scientists think luna moths evolved their long tails to deflect bat attacks away from the main part of their bodies.

“I thought, this is very bizarre. Maybe the genes that are normally responsible for wing patterns are here responsible for wing shape, because that’s seemingly the only thing that was transformed.”

Further adjustments to the timing of heparin treatment eventually produced changes in both wing shape and eyespots, overturning that initial explanation.

In polyphemus moths, the yellow borders around the two lemon-shaped eyespots on the forewings thickened. Brown scales surrounding those markings, which normally matched the rest of the wings, became whiter. On the hindwings, the black borders around the eyespots expanded. Together, these changes made the markings more conspicuous.

Luna moths underwent a similarly striking transformation. Their round hindwing eyespots took on a squinting appearance and developed thick, dark borders resembling mascara, turning subtle markings into a more noticeable display. Both heparin and dextran sulfate also changed the shape of luna moth wings, something not previously achieved experimentally in Lepidoptera, the group that includes all moths and butterflies.

“Some giant silk moths have eyespots that make them appear threatening to would-be predators. Others look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. What’s amazing to me, and what I learned from this study, is how easy it is for these features to go from one state to another. They do this without big inventions by simply expanding or contracting existing elements to the point where eyespots look completely different. All they need is a slight increase in the amount of certain compounds at the right moment,” Sourakov said.

Moth and butterfly eyespots occupy different parts of the wings, a clue that they evolved independently. Sourakov’s original goal was to investigate whether the two groups used the same genes to create these markings or had independently arrived at similar designs.

He tested the responses of several giant silk moth species to sulfated polysaccharides, reasoning that similar responses in different species could indicate homologous eyespots, meaning markings with a shared evolutionary origin. Further experiments would be needed to confirm that relationship.

In nymphalids, the largest family of butterflies, eyespots sit along the wing margins. Giving these butterflies heparin early in development can eliminate their eyespots entirely. Yet in Sourakov’s earlier experiments with two giant silk moth species, their eyespots grew larger. He interpreted those opposite responses as a clear indication that the moth and butterfly markings evolved separately. After his initial giant silk moth studies were published in 2020, he expanded the work to include luna moths, better known for their long tails than their faint eyespots.

The changes in wing shape remain harder to explain, particularly because they have not been observed in butterflies treated this way. One possibility involves how moth and butterfly wings acquire their outlines.

Earlier in development, before those marginal cells die, another signaling protein called Wingless helps control the size of individual wing sections between veins. Wingless does respond to the two compounds. However, the wingless gene is mostly inactive by the time eyespots begin forming, which is when Sourakov starts his treatments. That timing helps explain why experiments focused on eyespots seldom change the size of those wing sections.

The gene can also be activated when damaged wing cells need repair, allowing new cells to grow in wounded areas. In pipevine swallowtail butterflies, it has another role in the development of their tiny wing tails. A landmark study published in 2010 showed that both cut and wingless are active during tail formation in these butterflies.

Sourakov suspects that the same genes may help form luna moth tails. If so, natural selection would have independently recruited wingless for the evolution of wing tails in moths and butterflies. Those tails serve different purposes. The small tails of pipevine swallowtails help visually distract birds by contributing to a false head effect, drawing attention away from the insect’s actual head. Luna moth tails are much longer, and their shape also affects how the moths fly.

“This is just my deduction, but I think it is very plausible and would explain why in butterflies or other moths we don’t see much change to the wing shape in response to heparin– wingless is not turning on at that stage of wing development in most species,” Sourakov said.

The ease of altering wing markings also suggests a possible route for rapid adaptation to a changing environment. If a luna moth’s leaflike disguise stopped protecting it, mutations that made its eyespots more visible could be favored under pressure from hunting birds. In principle, that could shift its appearance within just a few generations.

“If you are a smaller bird or a squirrel, you will think twice before attacking something in the darkness of the forest that looks like the eyes of an owl. Butterflies and moths are masters of such deceptions,” Sourakov said.

Reference: “Wing Shape and Color Pattern Modifications in Giant Silk Moths Using Sulfated Polysaccharides: Understanding Morphogenic Signals in Pupal Wings of Lepidoptera” by Andrei Sourakov, 21 August 2026, Evolution & Development. DOI: 10.1111/ede.70058

#6447. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

P. Lewin et al. Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and sun compass error. Science. 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.adz2542

#6446. A New Era of Bionic Vision? AI Helps Scientists Unlock the Brain’s Visual Cortex

Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.

Artificial intelligence could make future bionic eyes more precise and responsive by improving how electrical signals communicate with the brain. In a study published in Neuron, researchers used deep learning to control brain stimulation in a blind man, producing more accurate neural responses with less electrical current.

The findings could advance visual prostheses that bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves, stimulating the visual cortex directly to generate perceptions of light.

Researchers from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU) tested the approach in a 27-year-old man who lost his sight following a traumatic brain injury. At a hospital in Spain, a temporary implant containing 96 electrodes stimulated his visual cortex, producing phosphenes, perceived as flashes or shapes of light.

Led in part by UCSB professor Michael Beyeler, the team trained a deep neural network to predict brain responses to different stimulation patterns. The AI model also incorporated measurements of resting brain activity, allowing it to account for changes in the brain’s condition before each test.

The AI-designed stimulation patterns produced targeted neural responses more accurately and required less electrical current than comparison approaches. Researchers also found that recorded brain activity predicted the participant’s visual perceptions better than the electrical settings alone.

“Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image,” Beyeler said. “But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.”

The implant could both stimulate neurons and record their responses, enabling the AI to learn from actual brain activity. The participant also described perceived flashes, including their brightness, size, shape, and color.

The technology could eventually help people who lose their sight through injuries or neurological and inherited conditions. Beyeler emphasized those “who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision,” adding, “For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.”

Describing the international research effort as “a true collaboration,” Beyeler said the study demonstrated how computational models could influence experiments involving human participants.

“Building a model in the abstract is one thing,” he said. “Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.”

Although the research remains an early proof of concept, it suggests that future visual prostheses may work better by continuously adjusting stimulation to an individual’s neural responses.

“A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe,” Beyeler said. “It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.”

Reference: “Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex” by Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler and Eduardo Fernández, 7 August 2026, Neuron. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

#6445. Scientists Found the Secret to Real-Life Invisible Tech—and It’s Amazingly Simple

Northwestern engineers used AI to sift 20,000 designs for a drone built around a flaw in human sight.

Invisibility is the sci-fi dream. Whether a Klingon Bird-of-Prey or James Bond’s Aston Martin, it’s undeniably cool for an object to blink out of existence—or at least, as it appears to our naked eye. However, while impressive stealth technologies can render aircraft invisible to electromagnetic “eyesight” such as radar (and some have even tried to channel Q’s engineering genius), tricking the human eye has proved to be much more difficult.

That’s why engineers at Northwestern University tried a different approach when attempting to design an “invisible” drone. Instead of using a complicated system of cameras, camouflage, or other light-bending materials, they went with another, more simple tactic: Just spin the thing really fast. The result was the Phantom Twist, a palm-sized drone capable of spinning 25 times per second. At that speed, the human eye can't keep up, and the drone shows up as little more than a faint blur. Details of this new device, which weighs little more than an ounce, were presented at the Robotics: Science and Systems 2026 conference in Sydney, Australia earlier this summer.

“Most efforts to hide drones focus on making them look like their surroundings,” Northwestern’s Michael Rubenstein, who led the work, said in a press statement. “Instead, we asked whether we could design the drone itself around the way humans perceive motion. This idea of low visibility through persistent motion is something few people have explored.”

One of those “few” was Michael Dammar. Back in 2006, the inventor was working for Minneapolis-based VeraTech, which patented a y-shaped, boomerang-like drone that could spin fast enough to become invisible to a casual observer. At the time, the company saw possibilities for the drone in the realm of military surveillance, and a few years later, engineers at MIT developed a different kind of monocopter, though their version was very much visible.

To build the Phantom Twist, the team used AI-driven modeling to generate up to 20,000 drone designs that could fly. Optimization algorithms then rearranged the drone’s main parts (a motor, propeller, circuit board, counterweight, and batteries) to find the best layout for stable flight and, yes, invisibility. The result is an extremely small machine that looks just like a small blur against the background as it rapidly speeds around its center of gravity. But the drone isn’t actually invisible. Its disappearing act comes from a limitation in how our eyes process motion, not from anything that hides the drone itself.

“The human eye takes time to accumulate signals, roughly analogous to the exposure time of a camera,” Northwestern’s Emma Alexander, who was also involved in the project, said in a press statement. “When an object spins quickly, we perceive it as blurring out and losing distinct features. Because this new drone is almost entirely transparent, its few opaque components are visually averaged with the background for an overall appearance of a slight haze.”

The researchers hope the tiny drone will be a boon for inspecting infrastructure without visual distraction of passing drivers, for example, and also a less-invasive method for tracking wildlife. Although for the drone to truly help biologists keep tabs on elusive species, engineers will need to perfect one of the drone’s core weaknesses—despite its small size, the drone is mighty noisy.

Rubenstein hopes that future iterations of the drone will feature more transparent support structures and quieter propulsion so that the Phantom Twist truly lives up to its ghostly name.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6444. The Hidden Brain Mechanism That Makes You Love Coffee, Chocolate, Fat, and Sugar

Scientists have uncovered a previously understudied dopamine pathway that may explain how we learn to enjoy flavors we initially dislike.

A food can become more appealing even when its flavor stays exactly the same. Researchers at UC San Francisco have identified a previously understudied dopamine pathway that helps the brain learn which flavors are worth seeking out based on what happens after nutrients reach the gut.

The study, published November 4 in Nature, reveals how a slow chemical signal connects digestion with learned food preferences. The mechanism could help explain why people develop a taste for initially unpleasant flavors, including the bitterness of coffee.

Dopamine helps the brain learn which experiences are rewarding, but most research has examined rapid signals that appear within seconds of external cues, such as seeing a favorite meal. The newly studied “slow” dopamine system responds to events inside the body. When digestive sensors detect nutrients such as sugar and fat, they initiate signals that can sustain dopamine release in the brain for several minutes.

“We’ve shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens,” said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

Coffee provides a familiar example of how this learning may work. Although its bitterness can be unpleasant initially, repeated experiences can teach the brain to associate the flavor with caffeine’s stimulating effects. Once that association develops, Knight explained, “that coffee starts to taste a lot better.”

To isolate the brain’s response to nutrients from its response to taste, Knight and James Grove, PhD, who was then a graduate student, delivered sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid directly into the stomachs of mice. They simultaneously measured dopamine release throughout the brain.

Nutrients entering the stomach produced a strong, sustained dopamine response in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA. Although researchers already knew this region received dopamine signals, their role in learning about food was unclear.

“We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role,” Knight said.

The researchers next tested whether the pathway was necessary for learning. When they blocked it, the mice continued eating normally but could no longer learn that a particular unfamiliar flavor was associated with calories. This showed that the pathway was important for forming food preferences rather than simply controlling food consumption.

In a separate experiment, the researchers artificially stimulated dopamine fibers in the BLA after mice sampled a calorie-free flavor. The animals subsequently developed a preference for that flavor, even though it provided no nutritional reward.

Together, the experiments demonstrated that dopamine signaling in this region can teach mice to associate a flavor with the beneficial effects of nutrients. Artificial stimulation could substitute for the signal normally generated when nutrients reach the gut.

Human brain imaging provided additional evidence of a similar response. Yale psychologist Dana Small, PhD, reanalyzed an earlier PET study involving 13 men who consumed either a milkshake or a noncaloric drink. Nutrient consumption was associated with dopamine release concentrated in the left BLA.

In another experiment, Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and colleagues used fMRI scans to study 38 adults after glucose consumption. They detected increased activity in the same brain region, although fMRI measures brain activity rather than dopamine release directly.

Both the mouse experiments and human imaging studies showed substantially stronger responses on the left side of the BLA than on the right. This asymmetry was unexpected because brain circuits involved in basic functions such as feeding are generally considered to operate relatively symmetrically. Knight’s laboratory is now investigating why the nutrient-related response favors the left hemisphere.

Identifying this pathway may provide new opportunities to investigate how food preferences develop and whether they can be modified. One possibility involves GLP-1 medications, which mimic a hormone produced in the gut and can substantially alter eating behavior.

The researchers did not test these drugs, so their effects on the newly identified dopamine pathway remain unknown. Knight has proposed that GLP-1 medications might reduce dopamine signaling triggered by nutrients, potentially making certain foods less rewarding over time.

Such a mechanism, if confirmed, would suggest that future treatments could influence not only hunger and fullness but also the learned associations that make particular foods desirable.

“By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods,” Knight said.

Reference: “The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning” by James C. R. Grove, Anna M. Hakimi, Queenie Li, Jingkun Zhang, Heiko Backes, Bojana Kuzmanovic, Jaewon Choi, Violeta Ubadiah, Longhui Qiu, Zhengya Liu, Dana M. Small, Marc Tittgemeyer and Zachary A. Knight, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

#6442. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

M.C. Nesselbush et al. An ultrasensitive method for detection of cell-free RNA. Nature. 2025. doi: 10.1038/s41586-025-08834-1

#6441. Scientists Reveal How a Mysterious Brain Structure Keeps Memories From Fading

Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.

To understand a sentence, the brain has to keep earlier words in mind as new ones arrive. Working memory makes that possible, holding information for a few seconds so we can compare it with new information, manipulate it, and use it to guide our behavior.

We rely on it to follow conversations, solve problems, and decide what to do next. Yet sensory information fades within moments once a stimulus ends, leaving the brain with the demanding task of maintaining a usable representation of something that is no longer there.

In mice, researchers at UNIGE have found that this ability relies partly on the claustrum, a thin structure deep within the brain between the insular cortex and the striatum. Their findings appear in Nature Communications.

The scientists tested mice on tasks that required them to remember either a smell or a touch. Each animal received an initial stimulus, waited several seconds, and then received a second stimulus. The mouse had to determine whether the two were identical or different. By the time the second stimulus arrived, the first was gone, so success depended on retaining information about it during the wait.

Temporarily reducing the activity of claustrum neurons cut the mice’s working memory performance in half. To control these neurons at precise moments during the task, the researchers used techniques including optogenetics. This method uses specific proteins to make selected neurons sensitive to light, allowing scientists to alter their activity through an optical fiber. The intervention helped establish that the claustrum contributes to working memory rather than simply becoming active while another brain region does the necessary work.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” says study co-leader Alan Carleton, Full Professor in the Department of Basic Neurosciences at UNIGE’s Faculty of Medicine. “Moreover, disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself.”

Working memory depends on interactions across a broad network that includes the prefrontal cortex, sensory regions, the parietal cortex, the thalamus, and other structures beneath the cortex. These networks must preserve information while allowing the brain to continue perceiving, thinking, and acting, but how they maintain a representation over time remains largely unknown. The claustrum’s anatomy offers a reason to examine its contribution.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” explains Carleton.

Recordings from the mice allowed the researchers to examine how information was represented in claustrum activity during the gap between stimuli.

“Our live recordings of claustrum neuron activity showed that a trace of the initial information persisted throughout the entire waiting period,” says fellow study leader Ivan Rodriguez, Full Professor in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE’s Faculty of Science. “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time. Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

“Our discovery could help us better understand cognitive disorders in which working memory is impaired, such as schizophrenia or ADHD,” explains Carleton. “Identifying the brain circuits that allow information to be maintained over time is an important step towards understanding how these functions can be disrupted. We now need to determine how the claustrum communicates with cortical networks, and how this interaction preserves the fidelity of the representations held in working memory.”

Reference: “The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice” by Anindya S. Bhattacharjee, Maxime Juventin, Chieko Huber, Burak Unsal, Jean-Rodolphe Renfer, Ivan Rodriguez and Alan Carleton, 14 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78363-6

#6440. A 1.9-Million-Year-Old Secret in the Jordan Valley Could Rewrite the Story of Human Migration

New dating puts ‘Ubeidiya alongside the oldest known Eurasian settlements—and hints that early humans arrived in waves.

In a sun-baked stretch of the Jordan Valley, not far from the Sea of Galilee, the ‘Ubeidiya archaeological site has yielded hominin fossils long thought to belong to migrating populations that crossed what is now Israel between 1.2 and 1.6 million years ago. Their remains and tools were intermingled with the bones of other animals, many of which have long since gone extinct. Although the site was already ancient, it gave up one more secret when its geological age was re-analyzed using its rock layers. ‘Ubeidiya has now been found to be 1.9 million years old.

Long before it dried up, this primeval Levantine paradise was a freshwater lake. A stream that flowed into it left behind sediment deposits containing hominin and animal fossils. Also found at ‘Ubeidiya were tools made by hominins who lived on the lake’s shores, crafted from flint, basalt, and limestone from the surrounding area. The sediment originally settled in even, horizontal layers, but these were tilted when the center of the Jordan rift subsided. A kibbutz member accidentally discovered the site in 1959 while plowing, and excavations began the following year, with heavy machinery needed to expose its rock strata. Not until 2021, however, did archaeologists Omry Barzilai and Miriam Belmaker begin to suspect that hominin populations might have occupied the site earlier than previously thought.

Their re-analysis showed that the sediments had a more complicated history than once assumed. “The exposure-burial history that emerges from the model implies recycling of sediments previously deposited and buried in the rift valley…subsequently exhumed, eroded, transported and then redeposited along the ‘Ubeidiya paleo lake shoreline,” they said in a study recently published in Quaternary Science Reviews.

Together with archaeologist Ari Matmon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Barzilai, who teaches at the University of Haifa, and Belmaker, of the University of Tulsa, led a team of researchers in dating sediment samples. They used three advanced methods that proved effective on material that’s long been difficult to date. First, cosmogenic isotope burial dating established how long the rocks had been buried. This method measures the decay of rare isotopes produced when cosmic rays interact with rocks at the surface. Second, fossilized shells from freshwater snails of the genus Melanopsis were found in the same layer as the hominin-made stone tools. Uranium-lead dating, which measures the decay of uranium into lead, gave a minimum age for those tools.

The third line of evidence came from ancient records of Earth’s magnetic field orientation, which were captured in lake sediments that later turned to rock. The researchers compared these records with the documented changes in the magnetic field’s polarity over time, known as geomagnetic reversals. The comparison showed that the lake’s sediment deposits had formed during the Matuyama Chron. Chrons are intervals of time defined by their magnetic polarity, and the Matuyama, a period of reversed polarity, began at the dawn of the Quaternary. Together, the three methods pushed back the date of hominin habitation to 1.9 million years ago. This is about the same age as the Dmanisi site in Georgia, where Homo erectus settled before spreading through Eurasia. Dmanisi had long been regarded as one of the oldest known settlements outside Africa.

Matmon, Belmaker, and Barzilai have suggested that this age means ‘Ubeidiya may once have been home to both Oldowan and Acheulean cultures. The oldest stone tools made by hominin hands come from Oldowan sites in Africa that are up to 2.5 million years old. (Some more debated sites in Ethiopia and Kenya go back 3.4 million years). By the time hominins reached ‘Ubeidiya, the flaking and fracturing involved in stone toolmaking had advanced. Acheulean hominins refined it further and also standardized the process. Their tools were strong enough to be used as weapons or for butchering animals for meat. The researchers think Oldowan and Acheulean hominins may have coexisted in the region. They also think Acheulean technological advances in the Levant occurred earlier than assumed.

“The revised age has significant implications for understanding the routes and timing of early human dispersal,” they said. “[This prompts] a reassessment of early Homo biogeography, dispersal pathways, and the possibility of multiple or overlapping migration events out of Africa.”

#6439. Earthquake Faults Can Suddenly Become Almost As Fluid as Water, Study Finds

Scientists have uncovered evidence of an unexpected process that may allow earthquake faults to slip enormous distances.

Rocks along Japan’s Boso Peninsula have preserved evidence of an extraordinary process that may occur during powerful earthquakes. Researchers discovered ancient fault structures suggesting that clay trapped between moving rock surfaces became nearly as fluid as water, potentially allowing the fault to slip enormous distances with little resistance.

The findings, from a research team led by Professor Tetsuro Hirono of Osaka Metropolitan University, could help explain how some earthquakes produce the massive seafloor movements capable of triggering devastating tsunamis.

The researchers examined exposed rocks that formed in an ancient seafloor environment approximately 15 million years ago. Within an old earthquake fault, they identified unusual wavy and curved layers, along with swirling structures resembling vortices formed by moving fluids.

The team described these formations as “turbulent-flow-like.” Using fluid dynamics to analyze their shapes, the scientists found evidence that a process called thermal pressurization had caused clay within the fault to become fluidized.

Thermal pressurization occurs when rapid movement along a fault generates intense frictional heat. As water trapped in microscopic spaces within the rock heats up, pressure increases, reducing the frictional resistance that normally keeps the fault surfaces locked together. This weakening can allow much greater movement during an earthquake.

“Our analysis suggests that the viscosity approached that of water,” Professor Hirono explained. “This would have been a dramatic reduction. The fluidized state would have acted as a form of dynamic lubrication, causing the fault to weaken dramatically. The resulting large-scale slip would have produced a large displacement on the fault near the seafloor, potentially causing a tsunami.”

The mechanism could help explain the extreme seafloor displacement associated with some major earthquakes. In 2011, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck eastern Japan, with shaking and fault rupture lasting nearly six minutes. The earthquake shifted the ocean floor enough to generate a devastating tsunami. Although the ancient rocks do not establish whether the same weakening process occurred in 2011, they provide physical evidence of how faults may undergo dramatic changes during seismic events.

The researchers hope to apply their analytical methods to modern faults, using changes in the viscosity of fault materials to better estimate how far those faults might slip during an earthquake. More accurate assessments of fault movement could improve estimates of potential seafloor displacement and associated tsunami hazards.

“Understanding the change in viscosity in fault-slips may allow us to more accurately recognize the magnitude of fault slips, which would support tsunami mitigation efforts,” Professor Hirono concluded.

Reference: “Coseismic turbulence-like flow of fault material along the shallow portion of a plate-subduction-related fault” by Tatsuru Fukuta and Tetsuro Hirono, 27 June 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-57630-y

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6437. The Secret to Saving Shellfish From Acidifying Oceans Could Be Hiding in Crushed Shells

Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean acidification.

For a young clam, the surrounding water can threaten the shell it is trying to grow. When seawater absorbs excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, making shell growth more difficult and energetically costly for animals such as clams, oysters, and mussels. Acidic seawater can even dissolve shells. Larvae and juveniles are thought to be especially vulnerable to this process, known as ocean acidification.

Indigenous communities have long added crushed shells to coastal sands to help keep these ecosystems healthy. Research from the University of California, Davis now helps explain how this material, called shell hash, can protect young clams from some of acidification’s effects. Published in Biogeosciences, the study connects the chemistry of water between sand grains with changes in clam growth and gene activity.

At the UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, researchers raised baby Pacific littleneck clams in four conditions. Two groups burrowed in sediment beneath either non-acidified or acidified seawater. The other two experienced the same seawater conditions, but their sediment contained shell hash. During the 90-day experiment, the team tracked shell growth and sampled the seawater three times a week, monitoring acidity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen.

“We found that, on average, clams grew larger shells when shell hash was present in their treatment,” said study first author Hannah Kempf, an environmental scientist at the California State Water Board who graduated from UC Davis with a Ph.D. in earth and planetary sciences in 2024. “Interestingly, we also found that, on a genetic level, the ‘acidification’ signal was dramatically minimized when shell hash was present.”

The crushed shells altered the chemistry of the water filling the tiny spaces between sand particles, reducing its overall acidity and creating better conditions for shell growth. That finding places the protection at a very local scale, in the water surrounding the burrowing clams.

“Adding crushed shells removed the negative genetic changes that occur when young clams are raised in acidified water,” said study corresponding author David Gold, an associate professor of earth and planetary sciences at UC Davis.

To examine gene activity, the researchers collected samples of the clams’ mantle tissue, which produces their shells, after 90 days and used them for follow-up gene sequencing. The analysis revealed gene expression profiles, or patterns of activity across genes. In clams raised in acidified seawater with shell hash, those profiles were largely indistinguishable from those of clams raised in non-acidified water.

“This was the first time the question was studied from a genetic perspective,” Gold said.

Traditional ecological knowledge provides significant evidence that shell hash benefits shell-making animals, said study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz. In the Pacific Northwest, some Indigenous communities build large-scale structures that expand intertidal spaces, the areas of shore between high and low tide. These structures promote habitat for invertebrates and other marine organisms.

“For me, one of the interesting aspects of this research is the potential to engage more fully with tribes on designing projects that promote their long-standing expertise and Indigenous science,” said Schneider, who is also affiliated with the National Science Foundation’s Center for Braiding Indigenous Knowledges and Science. “If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices.”

Reference: “Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams (Leukoma staminea) by altering pore water chemistry” by Hannah L. Kempf, Alyssa J. Griffin, Gabriel Ng, Tessa M. Hill, Tsim D. Schneider, Sandra J. Carlson and David A. Gold, 29 October 2026, Biogeosciences. DOI: 10.5194/bg-23-7627-2026

The research was supported by a California Sea Grant and the Russell J. and Dorothy S. Bilinski Fellowship.

#6436. A 400-Year-Old Mass Murderer Led a Brutal Mutiny—and Became the First Corporate Psychopath

A modern psychopathy test, applied to a 1629 shipwreck, uncovers the dark origins of toxic bosses.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When you try to envision a “corporate psychopath,” the kind of individual who blends charm towards their superiors and sadism towards their subordinates to rise through the corporate ranks, who comes to mind?

Actually, don’t say a specific name. These guys can be very litigious, so let’s just focus on the vague and the deceased. You’re probably picturing a man in an expensive business suit, maybe having a loud, hyperbolic conversation on an oversized 1980s cell phone. Maybe he’s monologuing about how “greed is good,” or how they’re “gonna need to send the National Guard to take him out, ‘cause he’s not goin’ nowhere.” Perhaps the corporate psychopath you have in mind is busy fretting about whether his business card has lettering in Romalian or Silian Rail.

In other words, short of someone you’ve seen on the news, or in your own boardroom, your mental image of a corporate psychopath probably comes from the movies.

You may want to revise that. That’s because a new study suggests that the original corporate psycho predates the 1980s stock market antiheroes of the movies you love. He actually predates movies entirely. In fact, he died before the city of Boston was ever founded.

In a study published in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics, Clive Roland Boddy, an author and pioneer in the study of corporate psychopathy, has identified Jeronimous Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Company as perhaps the earliest documented example of a corporate psychopath. To understand why, one must delve into the dark story of the 1629 Batavia shipwreck and its mutinous aftermath.

The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, translated as Dutch East India Company and abbreviated as VOC, was a fairly unique venture in the business world at the dawn of the 17th century. At the time, expeditions for goods and resources were often funded individually, and the companies behind them lasted only as long as a single voyage. The VOC changed that by merging 12 existing “pre-companies” within the Dutch Republic into a permanent company that would not only fund spice expeditions but also manage supply and stabilize the market. Shares of the VOC could be publicly purchased and traded by Dutch citizens at various aftermarkets throughout the Republic, including the predecessor to the Euronext Amsterdam, arguably making the VOC the world’s first multinational corporation.

In some ways, the VOC resembled the multinational corporations we know today, with the same ruthless efficiency. Yet the world around it lacked the kind of laws and regulations that are at least supposed to keep the corporations of our modern world in check. In fact, the Dutch government backed the VOC entirely, allowing the company to have a monopoly over the Asian spice trade. It was an environment that favored the bold, the ambitious, and the unscrupulous. It was an environment that allowed a man like Jeronimus Cornelisz to seize his moment.

“Psychopaths have a narcissistic and grossly inflated view of their self-worth and importance,” Mike Dash writes in his book Batavia’s Graveyard: The True Story of the Mad Heretic Who Led History’s Bloodiest Mutiny, “...a truly astonishing egocentricity and sense of entitlement, and see themselves as the centre of the universe, as superior beings who are justified in living according to their own rules.” It’s unclear exactly when Jeronimus Cornelisz created his own set of rules to live by, whether in his poorly-documented childhood, or when he took up his apothecary trade some time in the 1620s and began battling with his local town council.

What we know is that by 1628, the death of his child and the subsequent scandal it invited (the three-month old had died of syphilis, and Cornelisz tried to argue the child had contracted it from a wet nurse rather than his own wife) led to the Dutchman selling his business and taking a job with the VOC. In October 1628, the Batavia left port in the Netherlands on a trip to the Dutch East Indies, with commodore Francisco Pelsaert as its commander, Ariaen Jacobsz as its skipper, and Cornelisz as a junior officer.

Pelsaert’s journal recounts that on June 4, 1629, “I was lying in my bunk feeling ill and felt suddenly, with a rough terrible movement, the bumping of the ship’s rudder, and immediately after that I felt the ship held up in her course against the rocks, so that I fell out of my bunk.” The vessel had run aground on Western Australia’s Morning Reef while Jacobsz was at the helm, and roughly 100 of the 340 people aboard the ship were killed in the collision. To date, there’s still fierce debate over whether the Batavia crashed “by design or accident,” as by this time, Cornelisz had charmed his way into Jacobsz’ esteem, and in doing so, had convinced him that a mutiny was necessary to depose Pelsaert.

Either way, as some of the roughly 180 survivors disembarked for the nearby islands, leaving only 70 (including Cornelisz) aboard, an opportunity arose for the original “hostile takeover.”

Cornelisz had originally been among the 70 or so who remained aboard the Batavia, but after nine days, he made his way to nearby Beacon Island. He found the survivors stranded there to be starving, dying of thirst, and feeling abandoned, since Pelsaert had left with the other officers in search of supplies and aid. Seizing his moment, Cornelisz stepped into the leadership vacuum, amassing a group of loyal enforcers, and stripping the now subordinate survivors of any means by which to fend for, or defend, themselves.

Cornelisz began a reign of terror that lasted more than two months, overseeing the execution of those deemed “too weak,” as well as those he thought capable of overpowering him. Supplies were hoarded for his loyalists, while those outside of his circle were dispatched in ever more public and brutal ways. His roughly 40 man cadre killed an estimated 100-125 men, women, and children, and the survivors didn’t fare much better.

“Furthermore, when the most murders had been committed,” Pelseart would write in his journal, “...they shared the women who remained, or rather whom they had meant to stay alive.” Cornelisz, who had singled out Lucretia Jansz for his own ill-intent, “made several articles to which the women had to be put on oath if they wanted to remain alive, that they had to be obedient to the men in all that they should desire of them.”

While all of this may read like the barbaric horrors of a bygone age, befitting a pirate’s pillaging more than a modern boardroom, Boddy’s study found that when Cornelisz’s actions are viewed through the prism of The Psychopathy Measure–Management Research Version (PM–MRV), a ten-item model he previously developed to identify contemporary corporate psychopaths, the mutinous, murderous junior officer of the VOC checked off every box.

Boddy’s article doesn’t recontextualize Cornelisz’s crimes to exonerate the man; there’s little debate that Jeronimus was a psychopath of some stripe. Nor does Boddy suggest that the existence of the VOC created or caused Cornelisz’s monstrous urges. Rather, it emphasizes that the profit motive built into the structure of the VOC “would have been too great, even for a careful primary psychopath” to resist. This analysis demonstrates that corporate psychopaths as we know them today “have been active since the start of the World’s first stock exchange, and first multinational shareholder-owned corporations.” What unites Cornelisz with the less-overtly-murderous corporate psychopaths we encounter today is the manner in which they both “utilise a similar modus operandi across the centuries and are motivated by greed, self-aggrandisement, and the desire to hurt, dominate and control others.”

In other words, to subvert a quote lamented by another lunatic, Billy Loomis in 1996’s Scream: corporations don’t create psychos. Corporations make psychos more creative.
